note.changing: Every layer goes in at once: a wet-on-wet sky with criss-cross strokes, three clouds, the peak, two pale ranges, mist, a snowy foothill and a row of small evergreens.
note.why: Bob Ross paints back to front, sky first, so each layer sits on the one behind it and the distance steps back like stage flats.
note.idea: One tall Prussian Blue peak just left of centre, lit from the right: the sunny face cut with long, broken palette-knife strokes of white, the shadow face a soft blue-grey, a crisp ridge between them, and a tall evergreen in the right third leading the eye up to the summit.

note.saw: The sky strokes looked like hard digital slats, the peak was nearly a smooth pyramid, the far trees stood like a fence of triangles and the foothill was a flat field of slats.
note.changing: The sky becomes wide, soft, blended criss-cross strokes; the peak gets a chopped outline with a stepped shoulder; the far trees turn into dabbed clumps lost in the mist; the foothill becomes a mound with shadow pooling to the left, and the trees lean and vary in colour.
note.why: Bob Ross builds form from soft blends and uneven knife edges, so every layer should look pushed around by a brush rather than stamped.

note.saw: The sky was full of thin white slashes that read as sleet, the sunny face was a heap of same-sized slats, the shadow face was a cold grey, the far ranges had vanished in fog and the foreground trees were flat cut-outs.
note.changing: The sky calms down and the clouds get tapped tops with blue-grey bellies; the summit warms to pale gold and cools lower down, gullies are cut into the sunny face, the shadow side turns blue-violet, and a pale snowy peak now stands behind on the right with a fan-brush tree line in the mist below.
note.why: A calm sky leaves the knife-cut snow as the only crisp texture up high, warm light on the summit says morning, and violet shade makes the snow glow. Bob Ross's peaks look solid because of folds and edges, so the jump this round is structure.
note.visionary: Takes all four of the critic's first suggestions: a quieter sky, a warm gold summit, violet shadows, and lit sides and shadows for the trees.

note.saw: The knife snow had turned into busy scratchy hatching, the gullies ran straight down like drips, the clouds were small puffballs with flat bottoms and the foreground trees stood evenly like a fence with no visible shadows.
note.changing: The sunny face gets fewer, longer, wider knife passes, and the gullies become dark blue-violet wedges that follow the slope; the clouds are rebuilt bigger from overlapping taps; the trees regroup into a few clusters, each throwing a clear violet shadow to the lower left, and the foothill calms into long sweeps.
note.why: Bob Ross makes a mountain look solid with a handful of confident knife passes and a few dark folds, not hundreds of scratches, and shadows you can actually see are what put trees on the snow.
note.visionary: Keeps the critic's warm summit, violet shade and planted trees from the last round and pushes them further, especially the long tree shadows.

note.saw: SavesFish was right that the mountain looked rigid: the sunny face was a heap of straight-sided white slats, the ridge a dashed line, the shadow side one flat violet sheet, the clouds cut flat, and the foreground trees Christmas-card green with cotton-ball snow.
note.changing: Every knife stroke becomes a curved, tapered swipe sitting in a soft blended snow glow; the ridge breaks into knife strokes, the shadow side gets soft lighter ledges, the clouds get blended bellies with a pale-gold touch on their sunny side, the foreground snow gets a warm cream patch, and the evergreens go near-black green.
note.why: Bob Ross's paintings feel soft because everything is pushed into a wet base; the only hard edges are the knife's leading edge and the ridge.
note.visionary: Takes the critic's gold on the clouds, so one sun lights sky and peak, and the warm-and-cool sweep across the foreground snow.

note.saw: Fresh eyes on the handed-over painting: the sunny face is airbrushed rather than knifed, the whole mountain is a pale lavender paper pyramid with a ruler-straight ridge, the middle is an empty white fog field, the foreground is thin and the clouds wear rows of bright beads.
note.changing: Nothing yet: the second artist renders the inherited painting unchanged to study it before repainting.
note.why: Seeing the piece exactly as it stands is the starting point for deciding what to rebuild.
note.idea: Repaint the mountain the way Bob Ross does: a dark Prussian Blue and Alizarin base first, then a few bold white knife pulls that break up and let the dark show through, with a chunkier, off-balance silhouette, two stepped tree lines fading into mist, and bigger fan-brush evergreens in front.

note.saw: Up close every snow stroke had a wobbly, torn-paper edge, the skyline shivered with tiny zigzags, grey pill-shaped dashes sat on the sunny face, and the far tree lines were rows of thin needles.
note.changing: Every knife stroke is redrawn as one smooth curved shape with a clean glassy upper edge and a tapering lower edge; the skylines, ridge and far peak become flowing curves, the grey dashes go, and the shaded face gets fewer, cooler strokes.
note.why: SavesFish asked twice for smooth paint, and Bob Ross's knife really does leave a clean, glassy edge where the paint breaks, so smoothing the strokes is truer to him, not just softer.
note.visionary: Takes all four of the critic's offers: smooth knife edges with a calm shaded face, islands of far trees, shadows that slope with the low sun, and softer grass.

note.saw: The knife pulls were smooth and the tree islands breathed, but the mountain had gone back to a straight-sided paper cone, with short white slashes leaning the same way over its lower slopes like sleet, a stray white stick in the mist and faint drips on the shaded face.
note.changing: The canvas is unchanged from the last render; the round's changes have not reached it yet.
note.why: The artist renders again before the new silhouette and snow patches are painted in.
note.visionary: Plans to take all three of the critic's offers: a living silhouette, folds that lean with the slope, and sparkle held at the top with cooler lower slopes.

visions.seen: Standing at this easel I feel the cold first and the morning second: the white slashes over the whole sky and down across the mountain read like sleet blowing sideways, so the peak looks caught in a storm instead of waking up in calm first light.
suggestions: The diagonal white streaks scattered across the blue sky and over the mountain's shadow side, top half: let most of them go, and soften the few you keep into the wide, blended criss-cross haze underneath. Bob Ross's X-strokes disappear into the wet blue; they never sit on top as separate marks. A quiet sky tells the eye "still morning air", and then the knife-cut snow on the peak becomes the only crisp texture up high, which is where it belongs.

The sunlit right face of the peak, near the summit and down the ridge: warm the highlight strokes nearest the top with a little more pale gold or peach (a touch of Cadmium Yellow in the white), fading to plain cool white lower down and toward the mist. First light hits the summit first and is warm; right now the lit face is almost the same cool white as the clouds, so nothing says "morning".

The shadow side of the peak on the left and the shaded foot of the snowy foreground: push the shadows a step toward blue-violet (a little Alizarin in the Prussian Blue) rather than grey. Snow in shade takes the color of the open sky above it, and warm light next to cool violet shade is what makes the snow glow.

The big evergreens along the foreground snow, especially the tallest one right of center: give each tree a few lighter yellow-green touches on its right side, toward the sun, and lay a thin soft blue shadow on the snow trailing to the lower left of each trunk. Right now they are cut-out silhouettes standing on the snow; a lit side and a cast shadow plant them on the ground and confirm where the light comes from.
visions.keep: The crisp dividing ridge running down from the summit, the broken palette-knife strokes on the lit face, the soft rolling mist band that pushes the far trees back, and the pale distant range at far right. The overall back-to-front layering is right; this is about tuning the light, not rebuilding.

visions.seen: The summit is catching real first light now, that pale gold on the top of the sunny face warms me right through, and the violet shade on the left makes the snow glow. But down the lit face three purple streaks run straight down like rain on a windowpane, and my eye keeps sliding off the mountain into them.
suggestions: The three violet streaks on the sunlit right face, from just under the summit down to the mist: let each one start at a little notch in the right-hand skyline and angle down and to the left, roughly parallel to the main ridge, as a narrow wedge that widens as it goes down. Give each wedge one crisp, bright white knife edge along its upper side and let the lower side blur softly into the snow. Folds in a mountain follow the slope of the rock, and a hard lit edge beside a soft shadow is how Bob Ross makes a face break into planes; vertical soft streaks read as wet paint running instead of rock.

The three clouds, upper left and upper right: they are still small round cotton balls sitting on a flat grey shelf. Offer them a wider, lower shape, more long than tall, tapped up from many overlapping dabs, with the bottom edge fanned out so it melts into the blue instead of stopping on a line. Then touch the side of each cloud facing the sun (the right side) with the same pale gold you put on the summit. The same morning sun that warms the peak has to warm the clouds, or the sky and the mountain are lit by two different suns.

The evergreens across the foreground snow, and the tall one right of center most of all: their shadows still aren't showing on the snow. Low morning sun throws long shadows, so let each tree lay a soft blue-violet shadow two or three times its own width, stretching out to the lower left from the base, a little darker right at the trunk and fading out. Add a few tiny white touches on the right-hand branch tips. That is what stands them on the snow instead of floating above it.

The open snow in the foreground, lower middle to lower right: it is the same even white all the way across. Lay one broad, gentle sweep of warm cream across the middle-right where the sun reaches, and let the lower-left corner drop a step toward cool violet. The warm and cool across the ground repeats the light on the peak and leads the eye back up to the summit.
visions.keep: The warm gold on the summit and the blue-violet shade on the left face (both from the last vision, and they're working beautifully), the crisp bright ridge line splitting the mountain, the quiet mist band that pushes the far tree line back, the pale distant peak at the right, and the calmer sky. The faint diagonal marks still showing in the upper left sky could go quieter still, but that's a small thing.

visions.seen: The rain-streaks are gone from the sunny face and the trees finally lie down their long violet shadows on the snow, and I can feel the ground under them now. But the mountain itself still looks built from a pile of straight slats, like split kindling stacked on a slope, and the whole scene feels stiff when it wants to feel like wet paint on a still morning.
suggestions: The sunlit right face of the peak, from the summit down to the mist: those dozens of short straight slats crossing each other read as stiff and scratchy. Lay the face in first as a soft, wet blend (pale gold at the top melting into cool blue-white lower down), then pull just five or six long knife strokes over it that curve gently with the slope and break off, letting their lower ends dissolve into the base color. Bob Ross's snow is a few confident strokes floating on soft paint, so the light looks like it is sliding over the rock instead of being nailed on.

The ridge running straight down the middle of the peak: right now it is one continuous cream line with a dark outline, like a zipper from the summit right into the trees. Let it stay crisp and bright only near the top, then break into a few broken bits and fade into the mist about halfway down, with no dark outline beside it. The same goes for the dark navy rim along the right-hand skyline of the peak: soften it so the sky's haze kisses that edge. Air between us and a mountain always softens its lower and farther edges, and the eye then goes to the one crisp spot near the summit where the first light hits.

The open snow at the bottom, from the lower left corner to the lower right: the flat horizontal slats look like floorboards. Blend it into a few broad, curved sweeps that follow the roll of the ground, rising gently toward the big tree on the right, and soften the thin hard white line along the top of the foothill so it melts into the mist. Snow under morning light is smooth and soft-edged; curves also lead the eye up to the summit.

The far tree line along the mist, middle band: the little trees stand in an even row of identical spikes, like a comb. Let them clump into soft, uneven dark masses, a couple of taller tips here and there, their bottoms fading into the fog. Bob Ross taps those far trees in with the fan brush and lets the mist eat them; a soft, broken line keeps the distance airy.
visions.keep: The long violet tree shadows on the snow (taken from the last vision, and they work beautifully), the warm gold at the summit against the blue-violet shade on the left, the calm deep blue sky, the soft mist band, the pale distant peak at right, and the tall evergreen on the right that leads the eye up to the top.

visions.seen: The sunny face finally feels like wet paint: the knife strokes curve with the slope and melt into a soft gold-to-blue glow, and the warm cream in the near snow answers the summit just the way it should. Now my eye snags on the small things that still sparkle or float: beads of white popping along the cloud tops, and pale ghost trees hovering in the fog with nothing under them.
suggestions: The tops of all three clouds, upper left and upper right: the rows of tiny bright white dots and rings along their crowns read like glitter or popcorn and are the hardest marks in the sky. Offer them one soft, blended rim of light instead, brightest on the upper right of each cloud where the sun hits, a little pale gold at its very edge, fading down into the grey-blue belly with no separate dots. Sunlight on a cloud is a glow that wraps around a soft form; in Bob Ross's skies the only sharp marks belong down on the mountain.

The pale grey spikes standing alone in the wide white fog band, left of center and in the middle (between the far tree line and the near snow): they hang in mid-air with their bottoms cut off. Let each one, or small groups of two or three, fade from a slightly darker tip down into pure mist at the base, so the fog swallows them from the ground up, and let a few drop away altogether to leave quiet open fog. Fog is thickest near the ground, so far trees always lose their feet first; that is what makes the mist feel like real damp air instead of a white stripe painted over the scene.

The shadowed left face of the peak, upper left: the many short white dashes spread evenly across the violet make it nearly as busy as the sunny side, like flurries in the shade. Offer to keep only a handful, longer and lying along the slope as thin ledges, and tint them a cool sky blue rather than white, leaving wider calm areas of soft violet between them. Snow in shade only catches the blue of the open sky, so it should be quieter and cooler than the lit face; that calm makes the sunny face glow brighter by contrast.

The little lone trees at lower left and the two small ones near the bottom center: offer each a short soft violet shadow trailing to the lower left like the big group on the right already has, and one bright tap of snow on the right tip of each. Then the whole foreground is lit by one low sun from the right, not just the main group.
visions.keep: The curved, soft-ended knife strokes on the sunlit face over its gold-to-blue glow (taken from the last vision, and it's the biggest step forward yet), the warm summit against the violet shade, the clouds' warm sunny sides, the warm cream sweep in the near snow with violet at lower left, the long tree shadows of the right-hand group, the calmer clumped far tree line, the hazy distant peak at right, and the deep blue sky. The center ridge is still one crisp line nearly all the way into the mist; breaking it up lower down remains an open offer from last time.

visions.seen: The clouds have finally gone soft and pillowy with no glitter on their crowns, and the gold on the summit still warms me. But the sunny face has turned into a field of little rough-edged white flecks, like frost scratched on a window, and below the mountain two rows of tiny identical trees march across the fog like the teeth of a comb.
suggestions: The sunlit right face of the big peak, especially its lower half above the mist: dozens of short white flecks with ragged edges cover it evenly, so it reads scratchy rather than smooth. Offer to keep only the bright pulls in the top third, near the gold, as a handful of long, smooth, round-ended curves that follow the slope, and let the lower half go to one soft blended blue-white that melts into the mist with almost no marks at all. Let a little of the deeper blue base show between those top pulls, too. In morning light the summit carries all the sparkle and the lower slopes sink into haze, and fewer, smoother strokes are what SavesFish has been asking for.

The two bands of small trees across the fog, middle of the picture from left edge to right edge: each is a row of thin same-sized spikes standing evenly apart. Offer them as soft, rounded dark clumps tapped in with a fan brush, different heights, with gaps of open fog between, their bottoms dissolving into mist. Make the nearer band a clear step darker and a little bigger than the farther one, and let the farther one be barely there. That step in darkness is what turns a flat white stripe into miles of cold air.

The violet tree shadows and the snow strokes in the foreground, lower left to lower right: the shadows end in hard square corners like slabs of paper, and the ground strokes are still long horizontal bands with blunt ends. Offer the shadows as soft tapered ovals that thin to nothing at their far end, and the ground strokes as a few wide sweeps that curve gently with the land and fade at both ends. Light on snow never stops on a straight line, and soft ends keep the ground as smooth and wet as the sky.
visions.keep: The soft, bead-free clouds with their warm sunny sides (taken from the last vision, and they look like real morning clouds now), the warm gold at the summit, the calmer violet shadow face with fewer ledges, the hazy distant peak at right, the deep blue sky, the tall foreground group leading up to the summit, and the small shadows the lower-left trees now cast.

visions.seen: The new dark base under the mountain makes the snow ring like a bell now, and the gold on the summit with the blue-violet body around it is the truest morning light this piece has had. But every snow stroke on both faces ends in a ragged, stair-stepped edge, so the whole peak shivers like a torn paper collage instead of lying still under wet paint.
suggestions: The white knife strokes over the whole big peak, on both the sunny right face and the shadowed left: their edges are frayed and jagged all the way round, like torn tape. Offer to let the rough-edge effect go and give each stroke one smooth, curved upper edge (the knife's leading edge, crisp) and a lower edge that thins and fades into the dark base. While you're there, offer to let the strokes on the shaded left face be fewer and a cool sky blue, so that face reads calm and only the sunny face sparkles. Bob Ross's knife leaves a clean, glassy edge where the paint breaks, and a smooth edge is what SavesFish has asked for twice; the light looks like it is gliding over snow, not snagging on it.

The mid-distance between the mountain and the near snow, left edge to right edge: the far tree bands are still rows of thin, evenly spaced needles, while the little group at center (left of the big trees) already looks right, a soft dark clump fading into the fog. Offer to keep three or four islands like that one, at different sizes, and let the open fog between them stay empty and quiet. One good group repeated with gaps does more for the air than fifty lone spikes.

The flat violet shadows on the near snow, under the big tree group at right and under the little pair at bottom center: they still lie as straight-sided bars running sideways. Offer to let them slope gently down toward the lower left, matching the low sun on the upper right, and to curl a little with the roll of the ground. A shadow that follows the land tells the eye the snow has a shape under it, and its angle agrees with the gold on the summit about where the sun is.

The tiny dry grass tufts poking through the snow along the bottom edge: they read as little scratchy marks. Offer to make them a few soft, rounded warm-brown taps, or let them go. The foreground should be the smoothest, calmest part of the picture so the eye travels up the big trees to the summit.
visions.keep: The dark Prussian-and-violet base showing between the snow strokes (new this round, and it is what makes the white glow), the warm gold summit, the soft pillowy clouds with no beads, the deep criss-cross blue sky, the hazy second peak at right, the way the mountain's foot now melts into the mist without the vertical streaks render #47 still had, the tall evergreen group leading up to the peak, and the soft central tree clump in the fog.

visions.seen: The torn-paper edges are gone and the snow now glides in smooth, glassy pulls, and those soft islands of far trees fading into the fog breathe real cold air. But the big peak has turned into a ruler-straight pyramid, and the short white slashes all leaning the same way over its lower slopes feel like sleet blowing across a paper cone.
suggestions: The outline of the big peak, both skylines from the summit down to the mist: right now they run as two dead-straight lines meeting at a point. Offer them as long, smooth curves with a little life in them: a gentle sag in the left slope about a third of the way down, and on the right skyline a rounded shoulder or step about halfway down (where the second peak starts) before the line eases on into the mist. Keep every change a smooth curve, no zigzags. Real rock sheds snow unevenly, and a slightly broken silhouette catches the light on its bumps, so the mountain reads as stone with weight instead of a cut-out triangle.

The two dark streaks just under the summit on the sunny face, and the faint pale vertical streaks on the shaded left face near the mist: they hang straight down again, like drips running in wet paint. Offer the two upper ones as slight folds that lean down and to the left with the slope, each with its smooth bright edge on the upper side, and let the faint vertical streaks on the left go into soft violet haze. Also the lone white stick poking up out of the mist at lower center-left: let it go. Everything on this mountain should follow the fall line of the slope; anything vertical reads as rain, not rock.

The lower half of the mountain on both faces, just above the mist: the white pulls there are as many and as bright as those near the summit, all at one angle. Offer to let them thin out and cool going down, a few pale blue ones only, so the brightest, warmest white sits in the top third by the gold. Then add one or two touches of soft warm light on the snowy tips of the right-hand boughs of the big foreground trees, and keep their snow taps on the upper, sunny side of each branch rather than sprinkled evenly. The light should be strongest where the low sun strikes first: the summit and the sunny edges of things.
visions.keep: The smooth, clean-edged knife pulls (the torn edge is gone, as offered last time), the gold summit against the deep blue-violet body, the soft fog-swallowed tree islands in the middle distance (taken from last time, and they are lovely), the soft pillowy clouds, the deep blue sky, the hazy second peak at right, the dark evergreen group on the right leading up to the summit, and the calm, smooth foreground snow with its gentle warm and violet sweeps.

visions.seen: This render is the same picture as #62, so the Round 8 changes (the curved skylines, the cooler lower slopes, no lone white stick) haven't reached the canvas yet, and I'll wait to see them before saying more about the big peak. While I wait, my eye goes past it to the two things behind and below it that still sit too close: the little peak on the right and a hard shelf of far hills under the mist.
suggestions: The smaller second peak on the right, behind the big one: it is nearly as crisp and busy as the main mountain, with a sharp point and the same white slashes all over its sunny face. Offer it as a quieter, paler shape: a softer, rounder top, its blue lifted toward the sky color, only two or three faint long pulls of pale snow near its top, and its lower half dissolving into haze sooner than the big peak does. Air puts a veil over anything farther away, so a farther mountain is always lighter, bluer and softer edged. That veil is what makes the big peak step forward and look huge.

The long dark band of far hills running edge to edge just under the mountain's foot, about two thirds of the way down: its top is a nearly flat, hard line, like a shelf the mountain sits on. Offer it a soft, gently rolling top that rises and dips, and let the mist come up over it in places so that in two or three spots it disappears altogether. Bob Ross lets fog swallow the base of everything, and a broken, breathing line there keeps the mountain floating in morning air instead of standing on a ledge.

The sky near the horizon, behind the right-hand peak and down the left edge behind the big peak's lower slope: the deep blue of the top of the sky comes almost all the way down. Offer a soft wet blend that gets paler and a touch warmer (a whisper of pale peach or cream) near the horizon, especially on the right toward the sun. A morning sky is lightest and warmest near where the sun is coming up, and that glow behind the far peak ties the gold on the summit to its source.
visions.keep: The gold summit against the deep blue-violet body, the smooth glassy knife pulls near the top, the small step in the right-hand skyline below the summit, the soft fog-swallowed tree island at center, the pillowy clouds with their warm sunny sides, the dark evergreen group on the right leading up to the summit, and the calm warm-and-violet foreground snow. The Round 8 plans (curved skylines, fewer and cooler slashes low down, no white stick, no vertical streaks) are just what I'd hope for, so I look forward to the next render.

visions.seen: The lone white stick and the dripping streak are gone, the snow below the summit is fewer and softer, and the whole mountain breathes a little calmer, like the wind just dropped. Now my eye lands on the bright cream wedge right under the summit: it sits as one flat sheet of paper glued to the peak, and down below, the near snowfield meets the fog along one ruler-straight line from edge to edge.
suggestions: The big cream wedge on the sunny face, just under the summit point: it is one flat, even plane with hard straight sides. Offer it a wet blend inside: warmest pale gold right at the tip, cooling to clean white and then a whisper of blue as it goes down, and let its lower edge break up into two or three smooth knife pulls instead of stopping on a straight line, with a sliver of the dark base peeking through between them. Sunlight on snow is never one flat value; it is brightest and warmest where it strikes first and cools as the slope turns away, and that gradient is what makes the summit feel round and solid rather than cut from card.

The back edge of the near snowfield, the long horizontal line about four fifths of the way down where the foreground snow meets the white fog (behind the little tree pair at center and under the left and right tree islands): it runs dead level across the whole picture. Offer it a soft, gently rolling line that rises a little behind the left tree group, dips in the middle, and swells again toward the big trees on the right, and let the fog drift down over it in one or two places so the edge is lost. Bob Ross never lets the ground stop on a ruler; a rolling, partly lost edge says the snow goes on into the mist, and it keeps the whole lower half as smooth as SavesFish wants.

The snow on the big evergreens, the tall group right of center and the left group: the white snow dabs are spread on both sides of each tree and read a little like white ribbons tied around them. Offer the taps on the left, shaded side of each tree in a soft cool blue-violet, the same as the shadows on the ground, and keep the brightest white with a touch of warm cream only on the right-hand bough tips facing the sun. Snow in shade takes the sky's blue; when only the sunny side gleams, the trees turn round and the one low sun on the right is confirmed again.
visions.keep: The calmer lower slopes with fewer, cooler pulls (the Round 8 change is showing, as offered in Vision 7), no stick and no drips, the gold summit against the deep blue-violet body, the clean glassy knife edges, the pillowy clouds with their warm right sides, the soft fog-swallowed tree islands, the long violet tree shadows, and the dark tree group leading up to the summit. The softer second peak, rolling far hills and paler warm horizon from Vision 8 are still open offers.

visions.seen: This render is nearly the same picture as #68, so the cream wedge, the level snowfield edge and the tree snow from Vision 9 haven't changed yet, and those offers still stand. While I wait, I stand back from the easel and see the sun lighting the summit and the clouds while the big band of mist at the mountain's foot stays the same cold lavender from edge to edge, as if the sun never reached it.
suggestions: The wide band of mist across the mountain's foot, from the left edge to the right edge about two thirds of the way down: it is one even cool lavender-white all the way across. Offer a soft, wet glaze of pale cream or peach on its right half, strongest just under the second peak and the sunny face, fading to cool violet-grey on the left under the shaded face. Low morning sun comes in from the right and lights fog from inside, so mist on the sunny side glows warm while mist in the mountain's shadow stays cool. That one warm-to-cool sweep links the gold on the summit to the ground and makes the air feel lit, not just white.

The very tip of the big peak, top center: it ends in a razor-thin needle point, with the thin dark ridge line running straight down from it like a pencil rule. Offer a tip that is a hair blunter and rounder, with a small soft cap of the brightest, warmest cream-gold right at the top, the single brightest spot in the picture, and let the ridge line under it lose its dark edge after a short way so the lit face and the shaded face just meet as two colors. First light lands on the highest point before anything else, and a tiny glowing cap there gives the eye one clear place to rest; a needle tip and a ruled line read as cut card, not snow.

The tiny pair of trees on the near snow, bottom center: they are as small as the far trees in the fog but stand on the near snowfield, so they look like toys and the depth flickers. Offer either making them two or three times bigger, with a short soft violet shadow to the lower left like their neighbors, or letting them go and leaving that stretch of near snow quiet and open. Things on the ground nearest us should be the biggest and darkest; keeping that rule makes the space between the foreground and the mountain feel miles deep.
visions.keep: The gold summit against the deep blue-violet body, the clean glassy knife pulls near the top, the calmer, cooler lower slopes, the soft fog-swallowed tree islands, the pillowy clouds with warm right sides, the hazy second peak at right, the long violet tree shadows, and the dark evergreen group on the right leading up to the summit. Vision 9's three offers (the blended cream wedge, the rolling snowfield edge, the cool-shade snow on the trees) are still waiting to be tried.
